newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt cuts tariff rates, IMF deal looks on.
newsitem.headline: Egypt cuts tariff rates, IMF deal looks on.

text.p: The Egyptian government has cut tariff rates, clearing the way for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to approve a new standby credit agreement.
The Finance Ministry customs department circulated details of the new reduced duties to customs posts on Monday and they appear in Monday's official gazette, officials said.
Egyptian government newspapers ignored the reduction, which is likely to upset local manufacturers, and the gazette was not available at the government printer on Tuesday.
The maximum duty for goods other than luxuries falls to 55 percent from 70 percent, the officials said. They gave no details of the other tariff bands.

Economists familiar with the draft IMF agreement said the tariff reduction, the first since February 1994, was the last important piece that had to be in place if the IMF board is to endorse the agreement at a meeting in Washington on October 11.

If the IMF board does endorse it, Egypt will be very well placed to persuade its Paris Club creditors to write off Egyptian debt worth $4 billion, the third and last tranche of official debt relief agreed in principle in 1991.

The standby credit agreement would allow Egypt to withdraw about $200 million a year from the IMF. But Egypt, flush with foreign reserves of more than $18 billion, does not need the money and is interested mostly in the debt relief.

Arvind Subramanian, the IMF representative in Cairo, told reuters in August that other reforms outlined in the IMF agreement would promote the private sector, increase efficiency and raise exports to put Egypt "on a higher growth trajectory".

It envisages a serious structural reform effort, including privatisation, trade liberalisation, deregulation, greater private sector involvement in the financial system and modernisation of the fiscal system, he added.

The privatisation was an important element in it but economists close to the talks said Egypt would easily meet the targets on this through a crash programme of share flotations which started in the second quarter of this year.

Unlike the previous tariff cut in 1994, there has been little internal debate on the subject. It is likely to hit hard at industries such as car assembly, which will find it hard to compete with imports without tariff protection.
The debt waiver will reduce Egypt's external debt to about $28 billion and save the government about $200 million a year in foreign exchange interest payments.
